```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(dplyr)
library(apa7)
library(lavaan)
library(ggdiagram)
apa7_defaults(font_family = "Segoe UI", line_spacing = 1.5)
```

```{r}
#| label: setup2
#| eval: false
<<setup>>
```

Confirmatory factor analyses (CFA) and structural equation models (SEM) fit with the [lavaan](https://lavaan.ugent.be/) package are usually reported with at least two tables: one with the fit of the model to the data, and one with the estimated parameters (factor loadings, regression paths, and correlations). A CFA can also be reported as a matrix of loadings, like an exploratory factor analysis, and a sequence of nested models (e.g., tests of measurement invariance) as a table comparing their fit. The apa7 package makes all four types of tables:

| Table | Function | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| Model fit | `apa_performance` | *&chi;*^2^ test, CFI, TLI, RMSEA with its 90% confidence interval, and SRMR |
| Parameter estimates | `apa_parameters` | Standardized loadings, regressions, correlations, and defined parameters (e.g., indirect effects), under headings |
| Loading matrix | `apa_loadings`, `apa_factor_cor` | Standardized CFA loadings with indicators as rows and factors as columns, and the correlations among the factors |
| Model comparison | `apa_performance_comparison` | Fit of nested models (e.g., measurement invariance), each compared with the previous model |

The path diagrams in this article are drawn with the [ggdiagram](https://wjschne.github.io/ggdiagram/) package, using the standardized estimates from `lavaan::standardizedSolution`. The code for each diagram can be shown by clicking "Code".

# Confirmatory Factor Analysis

In the `HolzingerSwineford1939` data set from the lavaan package [@holzingerStudyFactorAnalysis1939], 301 seventh- and eighth-grade students took nine mental ability tests. The tests are thought to measure three abilities: visual (*x*~1~ to *x*~3~), textual (*x*~4~ to *x*~6~), and speed (*x*~7~ to *x*~9~).

```{r}
#| label: hs-fit

d_cfa <- HolzingerSwineford1939 |> 
  rename(V1 = x1,
         V2 = x2,
         V3 = x3,
         T1 = x4,
         T2 = x5,
         T3 = x6,
         S1 = x7,
         S2 = x8,
         S3 = x9) |> 
  select(-id:-grade)

model_3 <- "
  Visual  =~ V1 + V2 + V3
  Textual =~ T1 + T2 + T3
  Speed   =~ S1 + S2 + S3
"
fit_3 <- cfa(model_3, data = d_cfa)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-hs
#| fig-cap: Three-Factor Model of the @holzingerStudyFactorAnalysis1939 Tests
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: Code
# Standardized estimates without leading zeros
std <- standardizedSolution(fit_3)
lbl <- function(x)
  signs::signs(x, accuracy = .01, trim_leading_zeros = TRUE)
loadings <- std |> filter(op == "=~")
correlations <- std |> filter(op == "~~", lhs != rhs)
residuals <- std |> filter(op == "~~", lhs == rhs, lhs %in% colnames(d_cfa))

my_fills <- viridis::viridis(n = 3, begin = .25, end = .65) |>
  class_color(brightness = .75, saturation = .4)

my_cov <- redefault(
  connect,
  arrow_fins = arrowhead(),
  arc_bend = -.75,
  resect = 2
)



ggdiagram(font_family = "Roboto Condensed", font_size = 18) +
  {tests <- ob_ellipse(a = .5, m1 = 16) |>
      ob_array(
        k = 9,
        sep = 0.35,
        label = ob_label(
          paste0(rep(c("V", "T", "S"), each = 3), "~", rep(1:3, 3), "~"),
          color = "white",
          fill = NA,
          nudge_y = -.05
        ),
        color = NA,
        fill = rep(my_fills, each = 3)
      )} +
  {abilities <- ob_circle(
      center = tests[c(2, 5, 8)]@center + ob_point(0, 3),
      radius = 0.8,
      label = ob_label(
        c("Visual", "Textual", "Speed"),
        color = "white",
        fill = NA
      ),
      fill = my_fills,
      color = NA
    )} +
  connect(
    abilities[rep(1:3, each = 3)],
    tests,
    resect = 2,
    linewidth = .35,
    label_sloped = FALSE,
    label = ob_label(lbl(loadings$est.std), 
                     size = 13, 
                     color = tests@fill, 
                     position = .48,
                     label.padding = ggplot2::margin(t = 1.5))
  )@set_label_y() +
  my_cov(
    abilities[c(1, 2, 1)],
    abilities[c(2, 3, 3)],
    resect = 2,
    linewidth = .35,
    label = ob_label(
      lbl(correlations$est.std),
      size = 13,
      color = purrr::map2_chr(abilities[c(2, 3, 3)]@fill, 
                              abilities[c(2, 3, 3)]@fill, 
                              \(x, y) mean_color(c(x, y)))
    )
  ) +
  ob_variance(
    tests,
    where = "south",
    resect = 1,
    theta = 60,
    looseness = 1.5,
    bend = -15,
    linewidth = .35,
    label = ob_label(lbl(residuals$est.std), size = 11, color = tests@fill),
    color = tests@fill
  )
```

## Model fit

`apa_performance` displays the fit indices that are most often reported. A list of models gives one row per model, so the three-factor model can be compared with a model in which a single general factor accounts for all nine tests:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-hs-performance
#| tbl-cap: "Fit of the One-Factor and Three-Factor Models of the Ability Tests"
model_1 <- "g =~ V1 + V2 + V3 + T1 + T2 + T3 + S1 + S2 + S3"
fit_1 <- cfa(model_1, data = d_cfa)

apa_performance(
  list(`One factor` = fit_1, `Three factors` = fit_3)
) |> 
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)

```

The three-factor model fits much better than the one-factor model, though by conventional standards (e.g., CFI &ge; .95, RMSEA &le; .06) its fit is only fair. The values come from `lavaan::fitMeasures`. The table note gives the sample size and the estimator and defines the abbreviations:

Other metrics can be chosen with `metrics` (e.g., `metrics = c("Chi2", "Chi2_df", "p_Chi2", "CFI", "AIC", "BIC")`), and `metrics = "all"` shows all of them.

## Parameter estimates

`apa_parameters` displays fully standardized estimates (*&beta;*), with their standard errors and *p*-values, under a heading for each kind of parameter. Paths are labeled with arrows: a factor loading such as Visual &rarr; X1 is read "Visual affects X1," and a correlation such as Visual &harr; Textual is a two-headed arrow, as in the path diagram.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-hs-parameters
#| tbl-cap: "Standardized Parameter Estimates of the Three-Factor Model"
apa_parameters(fit_3) |> 
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)
```

Unstandardized estimates (*B*) are shown with `standardize = FALSE`. Here, the first loading of each factor was fixed at 1 to give the factor a scale, so it has no standard error or test, and the note says so. Other columns, such as *&beta;* next to *B*, *z*, and confidence intervals, can be added with `predictor_parameters`:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-hs-unstandardized
#| tbl-cap: "Unstandardized and Standardized Parameter Estimates of the Three-Factor Model"
apa_parameters(
  fit_3,
  standardize = FALSE,
  predictor_parameters = c("Parameter", "Coefficient", "SE", "Std_Coefficient", "z", "p"), 
  note = TRUE
) |> 
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)

```

Variances (labeled "residual" for indicators and outcomes), intercepts, and thresholds can be added with `variances = TRUE`, `intercepts = TRUE`, and `thresholds = TRUE`.

## Loading matrix

A CFA can also be reported in the matrix form used for exploratory factor analysis, with a row for each indicator and a column for each factor. `apa_loadings` shows the standardized loadings and leaves blank the loadings fixed at 0. As in exploratory factor analysis, the rows are grouped by the factor with each indicator's largest loading and sorted by the size of that loading (`sort_loading = FALSE` keeps the order of the model syntax). Suppose that Speeded Discrimination (*S*~3~, distinguishing straight from curved capital letters) loads on Visual as well as on Speed:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-hs-loadings
#| tbl-cap: "Loadings of the Three-Factor Model With a Cross-Loading"
model_3x <- "
  Visual  =~ V1 + V2 + V3 + S3
  Textual =~ T1 + T2 + T3
  Speed   =~ S1 + S2 + S3
"
fit_3x <- cfa(model_3x, data = d_cfa)

apa_loadings(fit_3x, communality = TRUE) |>
  # Recode variable names to test names
  mutate(Variable = case_match(
    Variable,
    "V1" ~ "Visual Perception",
    "V2" ~ "Cubes",
    "V3" ~ "Lozenges",
    "T1" ~ "Paragraph Comprehension",
    "T2" ~ "Sentence Completion",
    "T3" ~ "Word Meaning",
    "S1" ~ "Speeded Addition",
    "S2" ~ "Speeded Counting of Dots",
    "S3" ~ "Speeded Discrimination"
  )) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)
```

The communality (*h*^2^) is the proportion of variance in each indicator explained by the factors (*R*^2^). Rows for the variance explained by each factor can be added with `variance = TRUE`, and `apa_factor_cor` shows the correlations among the factors:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-hs-factor-cor
#| tbl-cap: "Correlations Among the Visual, Textual, and Speed Factors"
apa_factor_cor(fit_3x) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)
```

## Robust estimation and missing data

When the model is fit with a robust estimator (e.g., `estimator = "MLR"`, or `"WLSMV"` for ordinal indicators), `apa_performance` shows the scaled *&chi;*^2^ test and the robust versions of CFI, TLI, and RMSEA, and the note says so. With `missing = "fiml"`, the note also says that missing data were handled with full information maximum likelihood.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-hs-mlr
#| tbl-cap: "Fit of the Three-Factor Model With Robust Maximum Likelihood Estimation"
fit_mlr <- cfa(
  model_3,
  data = d_cfa,
  estimator = "MLR",
  missing = "fiml"
)
apa_performance(fit_mlr) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)
```

## Comparing nested models: measurement invariance

Do the tests measure the same abilities in the same way at both schools in the study (Pasteur and Grant-White)? A measurement invariance analysis fits a sequence of multiple-group models, each more constrained than the one before it:

1. **Configural**: the same factor structure in both groups
2. **Metric**: loadings equal across groups (`group.equal = "loadings"`)
3. **Scalar**: loadings and intercepts equal across groups

```{r}
#| label: hs-invariance-fit
d_mi <- d_cfa |>
  mutate(school = HolzingerSwineford1939$school)

fit_configural <- cfa(model_3, data = d_mi, group = "school")
fit_metric <- cfa(model_3, data = d_mi, group = "school",
                  group.equal = "loadings")
fit_scalar <- cfa(model_3, data = d_mi, group = "school",
                  group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts"))
```

`apa_performance_comparison` shows the fit of each model, and compares each model with the one before it. The comparison has the *&chi;*^2^ difference test from `lavaan::lavTestLRT` and the changes in CFI and RMSEA, which are often used alongside it because the *&chi;*^2^ test is sensitive to sample size. The models should be listed from the least to the most constrained.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-hs-invariance
#| apa7-width: landscape
#| tbl-cap: "Measurement Invariance of the Three-Factor Model Across Schools"
apa_performance_comparison(
  Configural = fit_configural,
  Metric = fit_metric,
  Scalar = fit_scalar
) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)
```

Constraining the loadings to be equal did not worsen the fit much, so metric invariance is plausible. Constraining the intercepts worsened the fit considerably [e.g., a drop in CFI larger than the .01 suggested by @cheungEvaluatingGoodnessofFitIndexes2002], so scalar invariance does not hold: at least some tests have different intercepts at the two schools.

With a robust estimator (e.g., `estimator = "MLR"`), the difference test is scaled (e.g., the Satorra–Bentler scaled difference test), and the note names it. Other metrics, such as `"deltaTLI"` and `"deltaSRMR"`, can be chosen with `metrics`, and `metrics = "all"` shows all of them.

## Multiple-group parameter estimates

`apa_parameters` shows the estimates of a multiple-group model side by side, with a column spanner for each group, so the groups can be compared row by row. Here are the estimates of the metric model:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-hs-metric-parameters
#| tbl-cap: "Parameter Estimates of the Metric Invariance Model by School"
apa_parameters(fit_metric) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)
```

The note gives the size of each group and says which parameters were constrained to be equal. The unstandardized loadings of the metric model are equal at the two schools, but the standardized loadings differ, because each school's estimates are standardized with that school's variances. With many groups, or with more columns, `groups = "rows"` stacks the groups, each under a heading.

# Structural Equation Models

Does industrialization lead to democracy? In the classic `PoliticalDemocracy` data set [@bollenStructuralEquationsLatent1989] from the lavaan package, industrialization in 1960 was measured in 75 developing countries with three indicators (*x*~1~ to *x*~3~), and political democracy was measured in 1960 and in 1965 with four indicators each (*y*~1~ to *y*~4~ and *y*~5~ to *y*~8~). The same democracy indicator measured in different years can share specific variance, so the residuals of matching indicators are allowed to correlate.

In this model, industrialization affects democracy in 1965 directly (*c*&prime;) and indirectly, through democracy in 1960 (*a* &times; *b*). The labels `a`, `b`, and `c` name the paths, and `:=` defines the indirect and total effects from them.

```{r}
#| label: pd-fit
model_pd <- "
  # Measurement model
  ind60 =~ x1 + x2 + x3
  dem60 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4
  dem65 =~ y5 + y6 + y7 + y8

  # Structural model
  dem60 ~ a * ind60
  dem65 ~ c * ind60 + b * dem60

  # Correlated residuals of matching indicators
  y1 ~~ y5
  y2 ~~ y4 + y6
  y3 ~~ y7
  y4 ~~ y8
  y6 ~~ y8

  # Defined parameters
  indirect := a * b
  total := c + a * b
"
fit_pd <- sem(model_pd, data = PoliticalDemocracy)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-pd
#| fig-cap: Structural Model of Industrialization and Democracy
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: Code
std_pd <- standardizedSolution(fit_pd)
path <- function(lhs, rhs) {
  std_pd |> 
    filter(op == "~", lhs == !!lhs, rhs == !!rhs) |> 
    pull(est.std) |> 
    lbl()
}
disturbance <- function(x) {
  std_pd |> 
    filter(op == "~~", lhs == x, rhs == x) |> 
    pull(est.std) |> 
    lbl()
}

lb <- redefault(
  ob_label,
  nudge_y = -.1,
  fill = NA,
  color = "white",
  size = 14,
  lineheight = .95
)
lat <- redefault(ob_circle, radius = 1.5, color = NA)

plb <- redefault(ob_label, size = 11, position = .47)

ggdiagram(font_family = "Roboto Condensed", font_size = 16) +
  {
    ind60 <- lat(
      fill = my_fills[1],
      label = lb("Industrialization<br>1960"))
  } +
  {
    dem60 <- lat(
      fill = my_fills[2], 
      label = lb("Democracy<br>1960")
    ) |>
      place(ind60, degree(30), sep = 2.5)
  } +
  {
    dem65 <- lat(
      fill = my_fills[3],
      label = lb(
        "Democracy<br>1965",
        nudge_y = -.1,
        fill = NA,
        color = "white",
        size = 15
      )
    ) |>
      place(dem60, degree(-30), sep = 2.5)
  } +
  connect(
    ind60,
    dem60,
    resect = 2,
    label_sloped = TRUE,
    label = plb(
      paste0("*a* = ", path("dem60", "ind60")), 
      color = mean_color(c(ind60@fill, dem60@fill))
      )
  ) +
  connect(
    dem60,
    dem65,
    resect = 2,
    label_sloped = TRUE,
    label = plb(
      paste0("*b* = ", path("dem65", "dem60")),
      color = mean_color(c(dem60@fill, dem65@fill))
      )
  ) +
  connect(
    ind60,
    dem65,
    resect = 2,
    label_sloped = TRUE,
    label = plb(
      paste0("*c*&prime; = ", path("dem65", "ind60")),
      position = .5,
      color = mean_color(c(ind60@fill, dem65@fill))
    )
  ) +
  ob_variance(
    dem60,
    where = "north",
    resect = 2,
    looseness = 1.1,
    color = dem60@fill,
    label = ob_label(
      disturbance("dem60"), 
      color = dem60@fill, 
      size = 11)
  ) +
  ob_variance(
    dem65,
    where = "east",
    resect = 2,
    looseness = 1.1,
    color = dem65@fill,
    label = ob_label(
      disturbance("dem65"), 
      color = dem65@fill, 
      size = 11)
  )
```

For clarity, the diagram shows only the structural model. The disturbances (the two-headed arrows on the democracy factors) are the proportions of variance not explained by the paths into them.

## Model fit

```{r}
#| label: tbl-pd-performance
#| tbl-cap: "Fit of the Political Democracy Model"
apa_performance(fit_pd)
```

The model fits well. When the lower bound of the RMSEA interval is 0, it is shown as .00.

## Parameter estimates

The parameter table has a section for each kind of parameter in the model: the measurement model's loadings, the structural model's regressions, the correlated residuals, and the defined parameters. Regressions are labeled with the arrow pointing from predictor to outcome (Dem65 &larr; Dem60 is read "Dem65 is predicted by Dem60").

```{r}
#| label: tbl-pd-parameters
#| tbl-cap: "Standardized Parameter Estimates of the Political Democracy Model With Significance Stars"
tbl_pd <- apa_parameters(fit_pd, starred = "p")
tbl_pd
```

Most of industrialization's effect on democracy in 1965 is indirect: industrialization predicts democracy in 1960, which strongly predicts democracy in 1965.

## Bootstrapped indirect effects

Because the sampling distribution of an indirect effect is usually skewed, indirect effects are often tested with bootstrapped confidence intervals. With `se = "bootstrap"`, lavaan's unstandardized confidence intervals are bootstrap percentile intervals. Show them with `standardize = FALSE` and `"CI"`:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-pd-bootstrap
#| tbl-cap: "Parameter Estimates of the Political Democracy Model With Bootstrap Confidence Intervals"
#| warning: false
set.seed(2026)
fit_pd_boot <- sem(
  model_pd,
  data = PoliticalDemocracy,
  se = "bootstrap",
  bootstrap = 500
)
apa_parameters(
  fit_pd_boot,
  standardize = FALSE,
  predictor_parameters = c("Parameter", "Coefficient", "SE", "CI", "Std_Coefficient")
) |> 
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)

```

The interval for the indirect effect excludes 0. The note gives the number of bootstrap samples that lavaan used and says that the intervals are percentile intervals:

# Table Notes

As with other apa7 tables, `apa_note` writes the note from what the table records, and the note can be used in the `apa-note` chunk option with [apaquarto](https://wjschne.github.io/apaquarto/) (make the table in an earlier chunk, and write `apa7::apa_note`):

```{r}
#| label: tbl-pd
#| tbl-cap: Standardized Parameter Estimates of the Political Democracy Model
#| apa-note: !expr apa7::apa_note(tbl_pd)
#| echo: fenced
tbl_pd
```

Without apaquarto, `apa_flextable(tbl, note = TRUE)` puts the note below the table.
